summary: Brick range lights on the Cape Fear River near Southport, lit by 1850; the front tower survives on industrial land, closed to visitors.

lens.where: two sixth-order lenses replaced sixteen reflectors by the 1855 report

structures.note: 20 ft (6 m), round, no lantern (Rowlett). Front tower still stands; the Society's record says only its bottom remains.

structures.type: square brick house with lantern room
structures.note: 35 ft overall per LighthouseFriends; torn down by the end of the 19th century after storm damage

access.note: On land owned by Archer Daniels Midland; no public access. Distant view from the Southport-Fort Fisher ferry.

facts.agency: Private (Archer Daniels Midland owns the land)

events.note: Front range tower dated 1849 (Rowlett); LighthouseFriends says both lights were built in 1849 and 1850
Station established 1850 (Society's record). The Society's lens entry says 1851; Wikipedia gives 4 January 1851 but its source was not read
Inspector took three lamps out of each beacon, finding they shone only on the land
Two sixth-order lenses replaced sixteen 14-inch reflectors
A Confederate captain's tour of the Cape Fear defences named Price's Creek on his route; the account is the Richmond Whig's, as the Hillsborough Recorder summarised it
Inactive since 1861 (Rowlett). Other sources give 1867 (see notes_for_editor).
A Union vessel left its anchorage at Price's Creek and threw several shells toward a Confederate fort, reported 2 February 1865
Discontinued 1867 (Society's record). Lighthouse Board proposed new towers in 1867, apparently not carried out (LighthouseFriends).
Robert M. Ruark, the keeper's son, fell when the tower stairs gave way and died about thirty minutes later (LighthouseFriends, second-hand)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1855 Treasury inspector's report shows the Price's Creek beacons in service by the first quarter of 1854, which fits the Society's 1850 establishment date. Wikipedia's 4 January 1851 date cites a 1851 Wilmington newspaper that was not read, so it is not used.

notes_for_editor: (1) Roster matched by name only: the Society's coordinates for Prices Creek Range Front (printed as 33 93.60' and 77 98.97', malformed; they place it inland, far from the river) are set aside; our record's coordinates agree with Wikipedia and LighthouseFriends and are kept. The keeper list matches LighthouseFriends exactly, which supports the identity. (2) Disagreements the story states: rear light square (LighthouseFriends) against the octagon tower in the 1850 specification; end of the lights 1861 (Rowlett, Wikipedia) against 1867 (Society; LighthouseFriends' 1867 proposal). (3) Society's record says 'Only Bottom of Rubble Tower Remains' and 'Keeper's Quarters?: No' and 'Year Original Lens Installed: 1851'; LighthouseFriends and Rowlett show the front tower standing and the 1855 lenses; the story follows the primary and LighthouseFriends. (4) Record's deactivated 1860 has no source we read; Rowlett says 1861. (5) Tower height 7.9 m (record) is the current height on Wikipedia, which says the tower was raised after 1917 (Wikipedia unsourced); Rowlett and LighthouseFriends give 20 ft (6 m) for the front tower; the record's structure entry is not corrected here. (6) Not used: Wikipedia's contractor, brick import and 4 January 1851 first light (its sources are a 1850 and 1851 Wilmington Chronicle and a newspapers.com page, not read). (7) LighthouseFriends' statements on the Ruark family, the Confederate signal station, the 1867 proposal, the 1947 owner and the 1868 death are second-hand; the Ruark daughter's recollection and the 1868 death are unverified beyond LighthouseFriends. (8) The Treasury 1855 citation is by question number; the printed page was not read. (9) The Hillsborough Recorder reports a captain's report that it attributes to 'the Whig'; it does not name the newspaper behind the summary. (10) Confidence medium: the keeper identities rest on the Society's roster and LighthouseFriends; the 1850s and 1860s events rest on newspapers and the 1855 report. (11) Fact check 2026-10-28: the Richmond Whig account reaches the story only through the Hillsborough Recorder (footnote 6). The front tower's survival is stated as a disagreement: LighthouseFriends and Rowlett show it standing, the Society's record shows only its bottom. Footnote 3 is cited by question number; the cached Treasury text has no page markers, so no printed page is given.
